sections.title: What top medical students actually do

items.q: Which study habits separate top performers in the ~700-student survey?
items.a: The top **5–6** habits drive most of the gap: **scheduled** calendar blocks, **eliminate distractions** (phone off, Wi-Fi off if possible), **study alone**, **3–4 hours/day** in **2–3 sessions**, and **≥5 days/week** consistency.
No — Huberman flags **correlation only**. Top students may study 3–4 hours because they're already strong; the habits are still the most repeatable patterns across contexts.

items.q: Why should you teach peers even in a competitive course?
items.a: Top performers **learn alone**, then **teach peers** in the same course — they do "exceedingly well" despite fears of giving away advantage. Teaching is a **mastery test**, not a freebie.

items.q: What is "watch one, do one, teach one"?
items.a: A lab tradition (surgeries, western blots, etc.): **observe → perform → teach**. Use it in **safe contexts** to move from proficiency toward mastery and virtuosity.

items.q: Why does focus feel limited by afternoon?
items.a: Focus is a **limited but renewable resource**. **Adenosine** builds while awake and degrades attention; **sleep clears it**. Schedule demanding study when you know you'll need that budget.

items.q: How long until a study schedule starts to "stick"?
items.a: About **3 days** of studying at regular times (**1–2 blocks/day**) entrains brain/body like sleep-wake cycles. Pulling attention back to the page is a **learnable skill**, not automatic.

items.q: What motivation style do top students report?
items.a: **Aspirational learning** — a broad, long-term vision of how success transforms self and family — pulls them through fatigue when material isn't exciting. When you **love** the topic, aspiration matters less.

items.q: Does easy reviewing work better than hard study?
items.a: No. Peer-reviewed consensus: study that **feels challenging** is most effective. Flow/osmosis myths fail; **effort is the cornerstone**. Quizzes aren't just grades — **retrieval practice** builds retention and offsets forgetting.
